title: Chapter 169 – Mei
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

He tells Ethan about Kito at dusk.

He has put it off all day. Yue's paper is folded in his sleeve, and he has read it so many times that the creases have gone soft. At the turn of the evening he goes down the stair alone, with the staff in his hand, and crosses the bridge, and stops on the platform with the cold mist at his knees.

Ethan Cole is awake. He is sitting as he always sits, hands cupped, head bowed. The seed in his palms glows faintly. When Jian's steps stop, he says, without looking up, You have heard.

"Yue wrote it down."

I thought she might. A breath. The silver girl. The one who listens.

"I have the page here. If you wish to read it."

No. He lifts his head. The gray eyes are red-rimmed and very old. I know what is on it. I was there.

"Then you will not mind if I say it."

Say it.

"The Seventh Door is under the valley, where you planted the tree." Jian keeps his voice level. "Kito holds it. He will open it from the valley side when the tree has fruited. And the Rest of All will wake."

Ethan makes a small sound. It is not a word. His shoulders fold in on themselves, and the light in his hands quivers, and for a long time he does not speak at all.

He was nineteen, he says at last. Did she hear that? He was nineteen, and I was thirty-one, and he laughed when I asked.

"She heard it."

He said that Mei's joke was not that bad. A cracked, wet laugh. It was terrible. She told it to him over lunch one day, when I was working late. Something about a chicken and a lighthouse. I never understood it. He said it was the best he'd heard all year.

Jian sits down on the cushions. "Tell me about him."

He saw things, says Ethan. That was all. He was a quiet boy from a family of farmers, and he saw things, and nobody knew what to do with him. He could look at you and tell you the day you would die. He told me mine. I would not let him say it aloud. The faint smile again. I never asked about hers.

"Did he tell you?"

No. Ethan shuts his eyes. Do you know, I have thought about that for six hundred years. Whether he knew. Whether he told her, and she kept it, and she has been holding it in her palm all this time.

The seed of light flickers, once. A very small voice, from within, says, I do know, Papa. He told me. And I won't tell you.

Mei—

It's a good one, says the girl, softly. Trust me.

* * *

The boy does not come back to the small round room until the middle of the night, and when he does, he is carrying a stone.

Jian feels him arrive. It is a soft settling, like a cat leaping onto a bed, and a warmth that spreads through the long cold dark of his chest. He has been lying awake on the eighth cot for hours, staring at the curved ceiling, listening to the Annex breathe. Seven children, asleep in their half circle. Nurse's slow steps in the corridor. The faint tick of the stove.

Brother, says the boy.

You are back.

I was at the table. A long time. A pause. I think I'm tired.

Rest, then.

I can't yet. The small voice is hesitant. I brought something. Can I show you?

Jian closes his eyes. The inner room opens in his mind, warm and low and lit by the stove: the rag rug, the stool, the window. On the shelf above the fireplace stand seven smooth stones in a row. And on the floor, in the boy's cupped hands, is an eighth.

It is small and round and the color of apple-wood. It is warm. It sits in the boy's palms as though it had always belonged there.

What is it from? Jian asks.

From the table. The boy sets it on the shelf, very carefully, at the end of the row. From Tao pushing the rice cakes at me. I wanted to keep it.

Jian is silent for a long time.

That is a good one, he says at last.

I know. The boy climbs onto the stool and looks at the eight stones. I wanted to tell you. In case you thought it was only sad.

* * *

The Hall begins to ring at the second watch.

Jian is on his feet before he knows what he has heard. It is not a bell. It is a low, steady, ascending tone that comes from the walls and the floor and the curve of the dome, a single note that rises and holds and falls, and rises again. The lamps in the Annex flicker. The sleeping children stir. Ao sits up with the rabbit clutched to his chest and says, in a thick scared voice, "Is it the beasts?"

"No," says Jian. His own voice sounds strange. "I do not think so."

Bell is already at his side, with her hair down and her smock unfastened. Duan Ke has his sword half drawn. Cheng Hui, in the doorway, has a pen in one hand and a look of fierce concentration. Yue is on her knees with both palms flat on the floor.

She looks up. Her face is the color of tallow. She holds up her slate, with a shaking hand, and writes a single line.

The Gate has stopped.

"Stopped?" says Bell.

Not stopped. Changed. The chalk squeaks. The pulse is not the same. It is slower. And there is something new under it. Like a second heart.

From the wall, from the grille, comes a thin high sound that Jian has never heard before. It is Mei. She is crying.

* * *

They go down the stair together, all of them, because nobody will be left.

The bridge hums louder than it ever has. The mist is thicker. The pale light that rises from the shaft has shifted, from milk to a faint gray-green, like the underside of a leaf. At the end of the span, in the glass chamber, Ethan Cole is awake. He is sitting bolt upright with his hands outstretched and his eyes wide open, and tears are running down his face. He does not wipe them.

The seed in his palms is no longer bright.

It has dulled to the color of a coal. It trembles. A faint web of cracks has spread across its surface, thin as hairs, and from the cracks, in tiny threads, a pale vapor is leaking.

Jian, says Ethan, hoarsely. Come closer. Please. Quickly.

He crosses the last of the bridge. The cushions have been kicked aside. The old man's hands are shaking so hard that the crystal floor rings.

She's at twenty-nine, says Ethan.

Jian stops.

Twenty-nine percent. It happened an hour ago. The memory, the sharing of the seals. It cost her four. I told her it would. She said it was all right. His voice cracks. I did the arithmetic. I thought, thirty-three, thirty-two, thirty-one. I thought I had room.

"What is thirty?"

A line. The gray eyes are wild. I didn't tell you. I couldn't. It was the Nine's protocol, the thing we built into the Hall in the first year. A fail-safe. If the keystone ever fell below thirty, the Hall was to begin to shed.

"Shed."

Terraces. From the outermost inward. He swallows. To lighten the load. To keep the Core alive. The sleepers on the outer rings are put into Terminal Rest. A mercy. They don't wake. They don't suffer. It is the only way to save the rest.

The word falls like a dropped stone.

"How many?" asks Jian.

Terrace nine first. Twenty-two thousand. Ethan's hands convulse. Then eight. Then seven. It'll go on until she is above thirty again, or until there is nothing left to shed.

* * *

Nobody speaks for a long time.

Jian stands on the edge of the platform with the staff gripped in both fists. The ringing tone has dropped away; down here, in the shaft, it is only a vibration in the soles of his feet. Around him the others have gathered, Bell, Yue, Cheng Hui, Duan Ke, the six children, in a half circle on the bridge. Zhen Li's lantern throws a small amber circle on the crystal.

A panel opens at the edge of his sight.

```
STANDBY :: Hall protocol SHED armed.
KEYSTONE COHERENCE :: 29.1% (threshold 30.0%)
SHED SEQUENCE :: Terrace 9 → 8 → 7. First release in 22:14:08.
OVERRIDE :: Operator Core feed. Rate: +1.0% per 7 days of Operator lifespan.
WARNING: Lifespan remaining: 19 weeks.
```

He reads it. He reads it again.

Nineteen weeks, says the boy, in a very small voice.

Yes.

That's not a lot.

No.

One percent is a week. The boy's voice is thin. We need one percent. Just one. That's all it would take to get her back over the line.

I know.

That's a week, Brother.

I know.

Then do it, says the boy. And then, at once, No. Don't. I didn't mean—

It is all right.

It's not. The boy is crying now, silently, in the room. I don't want you to die. But I don't want them to either. I don't know what to want.

Jian puts his free hand over his eyes.

* * *

"No," says Bell.

She says it flatly, from the end of the bridge, in the voice of a woman who has spent her life saying it. She is standing with her arms folded and her chin up, and her eyes are blazing.

"I have not said anything yet," Jian says.

"You do not have to. I know your face." She strides forward and plants herself in front of him. "You are going to feed her. One percent. A week of your life. And then the next day, another. And when she falls again, another. And you will be dead by the new year, and I will have spent my entire life as a healer keeping you alive for nothing."

"It is twenty-two thousand people."

"It is dead people. They were dead when we came." Her voice cracks. "Jian, they have been asleep for six hundred years. They have not breathed in a century. Nurse has been writing Rested in her book for a week."

"They are not dead until they are shed."

"And you will not die for them!"

The silence rings. Duan Ke has half turned away. Hai Ren has not moved. On the crystal floor, Ao has begun to whimper.

"Bell," says Jian gently. "I cannot walk away."

"Yes, you can."

"I have never been able to."

"Then learn." She seizes his sleeve in both hands. Her eyes are bright with tears and rage. "You told me that you wanted good months. Those were your words. You said you would let the children help. Well, this is the children helping. This is Ao, and Tao, and the rest of them, asking you to leave this Hall while you still can. You promised you would listen."

He opens his mouth.

Brother, says the boy, in a very small voice. She's right.

I know.

I don't want you to. A sniff. But she's right.

Jian looks at Bell, at her white knuckled hands and her wet furious face. He sees, behind it, the girl who once gave him her cloak, the healer who kept him alive for a hundred years, the woman who, when everything else was gone, was simply there.

He covers her hands with his own.

"I will not feed her tonight," he says. "I promise. We will think."

Her grip loosens. She sags against him, once, a brief fierce weight, and straightens.

"Good," she says thickly. "That is a start."

* * *

They hold council in the Annex, with the lamps turned low.

It takes the rest of the night. Cheng Hui lays out the arithmetic, and Ethan, from the grille, corrects it. Duan Ke asks what the beasts will do if a terrace is shed, and Ethan says, with great reluctance, that dead rooms are dark rooms. Zhen Li says that he can light terrace nine, if he must, and Nurse tells him sharply that he will do nothing of the kind.

By the hour before dawn, they have three paths.

The first is to feed. Jian's life for a week at a time, to hold Mei above thirty. It will buy a month. Perhaps two. It will cost him everything he has left, and the sleepers will still be shed when he is gone.

The second is to let the Hall shed. Twenty-two thousand will go, then twenty thousand more. The protocol is not cruel. It is merciful, in its way. But it will not stop until Mei is above thirty, and she cannot rise unaided.

The third is the one nobody likes to speak of.

"Take her out," says Cheng Hui, at last. He says it quietly, with his pen held very still. "Take the keystone out of the Gate and put her in the one place in the world where she can be held without cost. The tree. We have been avoiding the question. But I think we must ask it."

Nobody answers. From the grille, very softly, comes a breath.

I've been thinking about that, says Mei.

"Mei—" Ethan whispers.

No, Papa. Let me. The voice is faint and tired, and entirely clear. I said I'd answer, after Ao woke. I've had a long time to think. A pause. I don't want the tree. I still don't. But I think I might want what's inside it.

"What is inside it?" asks Bell.

A door, says Mei. A door that Kito is holding. And the mind of a boy of nineteen who joked about the way I told it. She laughs, breathlessly. Papa said something once, when he thought I was asleep. He said that Kito's door was the only one that wasn't a prison. He said it opened both ways.

Ethan has gone still.

That's not true, is it, Papa? You didn't make it up.

No, says the old man. His voice is a rasp. I did not make it up.

* * *

Ethan calls him back to the bridge in the gray hour, when the others have gone to rest.

He goes alone. The mist is thin. The chamber glimmers in the dimness, and the old man sits within it, cross-legged, a small shape in a huge dark. When Jian reaches the platform, the thin voice says, without preamble, You are thinking of feeding her.

"I am thinking of it."

Don't.

"You have not even heard—"

I have heard everything you have ever thought about that girl. The old man opens his eyes. They are gentle, and dry, and terribly tired. You think that because you are the key, and the Hall's chosen guest, and the last copy, that you owe her something. You do not. I do. I am the one who put her there.

"You cannot feed her. You are the cage."

I am the father. A flicker of a smile. It is a smaller thing. But it is mine.

Jian leans on the staff. "What would you have me do?"

Take the children. Go home. Plant what must be planted. The voice softens. I am sorry that I asked you to carry so much. I should not have asked. I did not think a man would come who would carry it.

"I did not carry it. I only followed the road."

Yes, says Ethan Cole. That is what carrying is.

The light in his hands brightens, faintly. A small sleepy voice murmurs from within, Papa, are you telling him to go?

Yes, sweetheart.

Good, says Mei. I was going to.

Jian laughs. It cracks in his throat, and turns into something else, and he has to put his hand over his mouth.

* * *

Cheng Hui finds him afterward, in the corridor, with a map.

It is a fine sheet of Nurse's paper, folded in eight, and he spreads it on the lectern with the care of a man laying out a surgeon's tools. It is drawn in ink, in his own neat hand, and it shows the Hall as a dome, the Wall as a line, and between them a long dotted curve, with small notes in the margins.

"I have been doing a little arithmetic," he says. "Of the geographical kind."

"Go on."

"Mr. Cole says the Seventh Door lies beneath the valley, and opens from the valley side. That is the direction in which we are traveling in any case. But there is a second thing I have realized, and I do not think anyone else has." He taps the dotted line. "The Doors are numbered along the Seam. From north to south. Door Six, here. Door Seven, there. They are not far apart."

"How far?"

"By the old measure, seven hundred miles. By the Seam, perhaps four." The young man's eyes are bright. "The Seam runs from Door to Door like a river between bridges. Mr. Cole's notes say that the Nine built tunnels. Narrow ones, for the keepers. The Sixth and Seventh Doors were meant to be linked."

Jian goes very still.

"Linked."

"By a passage. I have not found it. But I have found reference to it, in three different places. Door Six has a Seventh Door annex." He folds his hands. "I believe, my friend, that there may be a shorter way home than the one you walked."

Jian looks at the map. He looks at the dotted line.

"Where?" he says.

"I do not know." Cheng Hui smiles faintly. "But I propose we ask the stone."

Nurse finds Bell in the kitchen at dawn.

It is a small stone room off the Annex, with a clay stove and a rack of copper pots, and Bell is standing at the table with her sleeves rolled up, kneading a lump of rice dough. She has been at it for an hour. She does not look up as the older woman enters.

"You'll want to take the dried plums," says Nurse. "And the barley. The road will be long."

"We have plenty."

"You'll want more." Nurse opens a cupboard and takes down a cloth sack. "I am not going with you."

Bell's hands stop.

"I thought you might say so." She wipes them slowly on her apron. "I had hoped you would not."

"The Hall needs a keeper." Nurse sets the sack on the table. Her voice is soft, and entirely level. "There are one hundred and fifty thousand left. A girl of eleven who needs a friend. An old man in a well. And the lamps. They will go out, Bell, if I leave them. I have kept them for six hundred years. I should like to keep them until the end."

"It's not the end."

"It may be." A faint smile. "But it may not. And whichever, I'd like to be here."

Bell looks at her for a long time. Then she crosses the kitchen in three strides and throws her arms round the small round woman, and holds her, hard.

"You are the best nurse I have ever known," she says into the gray head.

"I am the only nurse you have ever known." But the hand that pats her back is trembling. "Go, now. Make your bread. Feed my children."

* * *

Duan Ke finds Tao sitting on the stair with his top in his hand.

The little boy is alone. He has crept out of the Annex in the pale hour before the lamps are lit, and he sits on the third step with his chin on his knees and the wooden top held loosely in one fist. He has not wound the string. He is staring at the floor.

The sword boy stops two steps above him. He says nothing for a while. Then he lowers himself onto the stair, with a faint clink of the scabbard, and puts his elbows on his knees.

"You're not sleeping," he says.

"Neither are you."

"I'm a soldier."

"I'm a rock," says Tao, with some dignity.

Duan Ke's mouth twitches. "A rock that doesn't sleep is a very bad rock."

Tao almost smiles. Then his chin trembles, and he looks at the top, and says, in a small tight voice, "I forgot how to do it."

"I know."

"What if I forget other things?"

"You will." The sword boy says it plainly. "Everyone does. I forgot my father's face years ago. I only remember the sword." He turns the pale blade in its scabbard. "But there's a way."

"What?"

"You pick the things you want to keep. And you tell them to someone. Out loud. Over and over, until it's theirs, too." He glances sidelong. "Then if you lose them, they're still safe."

Tao thinks. "Can I tell you?"

"Go on."

The small boy takes a breath. "I had a house," he says. "With a red door. And my mother used to sing when she was cooking, and there was a dog called Biscuit, and a window with a crack in it that looked like a river."

Duan Ke listens. When Tao has finished, he nods slowly.

"I'll remember," he says. "The red door. Biscuit. The window like a river."

Tao leans against him, a small warm weight. "Thanks," he whispers.

"Don't mention it," says Duan Ke, awkwardly, and puts his arm round him, and does not move for a long time.

* * *

The first terrace goes dark at the twenty-second hour.

Jian is standing at the rail of the eighth terrace when it happens, with Zhen Li at his side and the lantern held between them. They have been watching for it. They have been watching, in silence, for a quarter of an hour, ever since Nurse, with a face like stone, took her snuffer to the corridor lamps and put them out, one by one, to spare the oil.

The ring of blue light on the ninth terrace flickers.

It is a soft, slow flicker, like a breath. The beds below, row on row on row, tilt in the dimness. Their pale glow wavers, steadies, wavers again. And then, from the outermost row, the lights begin to go out.

One. Two. A dozen. A hundred.

They go in a wave, from the edge toward the center. The dark sweeps down the terrace like a hand drawing a sheet. There is no sound. There is no cry. The glow fades from the rails, from the brass numbers, from the faces of the sleepers, and the dark comes in behind it, and in the gloom, row after row after row, the beds grow still.

Zhen Li's lantern jerks in his hand. He has made a small sound in his throat. "I could," he says. "I could light it. I could—"

"No," says Jian, very softly.

"They're going out. They're all going out."

"I know."

"It's twenty-two thousand."

"I know." His own voice cracks. "I know, Zhen Li. I am so sorry."

The boy turns his face into Jian's sleeve. He is shaking. The lantern in his hand shrinks to a spark, and goes out.

Behind them, in the dark corridor, a small round woman in an apron is standing with a cracked blue ledger in her arms. She has not said a word. Her face, in the faint light, is calm. She opens the book. She dips the stub of brown ink.

And begins, line by line, by the glow of the last dying lamp, to write.
